theme.q: A yoghurt brand sells the same product in two shops. In shop 1 the label says “95% fat-free”, in shop 2 it says “contains 5% fat”. Shoppers buy it far more often in shop 1. Which principle of expected utility theory does this violate?
o: Transitivity
Invariance
Cancellation
Dominance
theme.spot: Same product, same facts, only the description differs.
theme.why: Invariance says a choice should not depend on how the same option is described. “95% fat-free” and “5% fat” are the same yoghurt, so a different choice is a framing effect. Transitivity is about a consistent order of preferences (A over B over C), and cancellation about ignoring outcomes that two options share.
theme.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2][LO D1, D4][IDQ DE6] Robinson-Riegler p. 482; Matlin pp. 437-440

theme.q: According to the transitivity principle of expected utility theory, a person who prefers a bike to a scooter and a scooter to a car should
o: prefer the bike to the car as well
choose the same option however it is described
ignore outcomes that the bike and the car share
value a loss of the car more than a gain of it
theme.spot: “Prefers X to Y and Y to Z, so…” asks what follows logically.
theme.why: Transitivity: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A must be preferred to C. Otherwise your preferences go round in a circle. “Same choice however described” is invariance, “ignore shared outcomes” is cancellation, and the last option describes loss aversion from prospect theory.
theme.src: [PAST-2] set2 transitivity item; EU principles as defined in set1/set2

theme.q:
Judge these statements.
I. Someone who chooses tea over coffee, coffee over juice, and juice over tea violates transitivity.
II. Someone who reacts differently to “€5 off” and “pay €15 instead of €20” violates cancellation.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Check each scenario against the principle it names.
theme.why: Statement I is true: tea > coffee > juice > tea is a circle, which breaks transitivity. Statement II is false: the two price labels describe the same deal, so the principle that is broken is invariance (framing), not cancellation. Cancellation is about ignoring an outcome that two options have in common.
theme.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2] set1/set2 EU principle items

theme.q:
Consider these two choices.
ChoiceOptionOutcomes
1A€1 million for sure
1B10%: €5 million; 89%: €1 million; 1%: nothing
2C11%: €1 million; 89%: nothing
2D10%: €5 million; 90%: nothing
Most people choose A in choice 1 and D in choice 2. Which principle of expected utility theory does this pattern violate?
o: Cancellation, because a chance shared by both options should not matter
Transitivity, because the four options together form a circle of preferences
Invariance, because choice 2 merely describes choice 1 in other words
Dominance, because option D is better than option C in every outcome
theme.spot: Find what the two choices have in common and what was removed.
theme.why: Choice 2 is choice 1 with the same 89% chance of €1 million taken out of both options. By cancellation (independence), an outcome shared by both options should not affect the choice, so A should go with C and B with D. People switch because A is certain: the certainty effect (Allais paradox). It is not invariance, because choice 2 is a different gamble, not a new wording of the same one.
theme.src: [PAST-2] set2 Allais item; Allais paradox as explained in set2

theme.q: What is meant by the certainty effect?
o: People overweight an outcome that is certain compared with one that is only probable
People value a loss of a given size more strongly than a gain of exactly the same size
People change their choice when the same outcome is described in a different way
People judge an outcome likely when it resembles the process that produced it
theme.spot: A definition on the probability side of decision making.
theme.why: The certainty effect is about probabilities: a sure thing gets extra weight compared with something that is merely likely (it drives the Allais paradox). Losses weighing more is loss aversion; a different choice for a new description is framing; judging by resemblance is representativeness.
theme.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2] set1/set2 certainty effect items

theme.q: Prospect theory has a value side (how gains and losses feel) and a probability side (how chances are weighted). Where do loss aversion and the certainty effect belong?
o: Loss aversion on the value side, the certainty effect on the probability side
Loss aversion on the probability side, the certainty effect on the value side
Both on the value side, because both concern how strongly outcomes are felt
Both on the probability side, because both concern how risky choices are made
theme.spot: Ask of each: is it about how much, or about how likely?
theme.why: Loss aversion is about how much an outcome hurts or pleases: the value curve is steeper for losses. The certainty effect is about how likely: a 100% chance is weighted more than its size alone justifies. So one belongs to the value function, the other to probability weighting.
theme.src: [PAST-1] set1 prospect theory item; [IDQ DE3] Robinson-Riegler p. 483

theme.q: The figure shows the utility (subjective worth) of total wealth according to expected utility theory. Which idea does the flattening of the curve express?
o: Loss aversion
Diminishing marginal utility
The certainty effect
Reference dependence
theme.spot: Each extra step to the right adds less height.
theme.why: Going from €0 to €1,000 adds much more utility than going from €4,000 to €5,000: each extra euro is worth less the more you already have. That is diminishing marginal utility, a concave curve. Loss aversion and reference dependence belong to prospect theory and need a curve with a gain side and a loss side; the certainty effect concerns probabilities, which are not on this graph.
theme.src: [PAST-2] set2 diminishing marginal utility item; illustrative curve

theme.q: Diminishing marginal utility means that
o: each extra unit of money adds less satisfaction the more money you already have
a loss of money is felt more strongly than a gain of the same amount
a sure amount of money is weighted more than an equally large likely amount
money that is already spent should not influence a new decision
theme.spot: “Marginal” = the next extra unit.
theme.why: Diminishing marginal utility: the next €100 means less to someone who has a lot than to someone who has little, so the utility curve is concave. The second option is loss aversion, the third the certainty effect, the fourth the rule that sunk costs should be ignored.
theme.src: [PAST-2] set2 diminishing marginal utility item

theme.q: The figure shows the value function of prospect theory. What would it look like if people showed diminishing sensitivity but no loss aversion?

chart.title: Prospect theory value function (illustrative)
chart.note: Illustrative shape after Robinson-Riegler Figure 11.4. Horizontal axis: loss or gain from the reference point (0).

o: A straight line through the reference point, equally steep for gains and losses
An S-shape that is equally steep for losses and gains, bending on both sides
A curve that is concave for losses and convex for gains, steeper for losses
A curve that rises only for gains and stays flat at zero for all losses
theme.spot: Remove one feature, keep the other.
theme.why: The real curve has two features: it flattens further from the reference point (diminishing sensitivity) and the loss side is steeper (loss aversion). Remove only loss aversion and you keep the S-shape, but the loss half becomes a mirror image of the gain half. A straight line would remove diminishing sensitivity too.
theme.src: [PAST-2][IDQ DE3, DE4] Robinson-Riegler Figure 11.4; illustrative values

theme.q: In a survey, employees say a pay cut of €100 a month would upset them far more than a raise of €100 a month would please them. Which concept describes this?
o: Diminishing marginal utility
The certainty effect
Loss aversion
Psychological accounting
theme.spot: Same amount, losing hurts more than gaining pleases.
theme.why: Loss aversion: in prospect theory the value function is steeper for losses than for gains, so losing €100 weighs more than winning €100. Diminishing marginal utility is about the next euro mattering less as you get richer, not about the gain/loss difference. No probabilities are involved, so it is not the certainty effect.
theme.src: [PAST-2][IDQ DE3] Robinson-Riegler p. 483

theme.q: The figure shows the choices in Tversky and Kahneman's (1981) Asian disease problem. One group chose between programmes described in lives saved, another group between the same programmes described in deaths. Which conclusion fits the figure?
o: Most people chose the sure programme in both frames, but fewer did so in the loss frame
People were risk seeking for lives saved and risk averse for deaths, as prospect theory predicts
The wording alone reversed the majority, so the choices violate invariance
The risky programme saved more lives on average, so choosing it in the loss frame was rational
theme.spot: Same options in both frames: what flipped, and why does that matter?
theme.why: In the gain frame 72% chose the sure programme; in the loss frame 78% chose the risky one. Since A equals C and B equals D, only the wording differed, so the reversal violates invariance. The direction is the opposite of the second option: people are risk averse for gains and risk seeking for losses. The programmes had equal expected outcomes.
theme.src: [LO D4][IDQ DE5, DE6] Robinson-Riegler Table 11.10; Matlin p. 439

theme.q: A wildfire threatens 300 homes. Residents must choose a plan. Plan 1: 200 homes will burn down. Plan 2: there is a one-third chance that no home burns down and a two-thirds chance that all 300 burn down. What does prospect theory predict?
o: Most choose plan 2, because outcomes framed as losses make people seek risk
Most choose plan 1, because people avoid risk whenever lives or homes are at stake
Most choose plan 1, because a certain outcome is always weighted more heavily
Choices split evenly, because both plans lead to the same expected number of losses
theme.spot: Look at the wording: homes saved or homes lost?
theme.why: Both plans lose 200 homes on average, but they are described as losses (“will burn down”). In a loss frame people are risk seeking: the sure loss feels worse than a gamble that might avoid all loss, as in the Asian disease problem (78% chose the risky option). The certainty effect makes a sure gain attractive, but a sure loss is what people try to escape.
theme.src: [LO D4][IDQ DE4] Matlin p. 440; Robinson-Riegler p. 484

theme.q: Which statement about expected utility theory and prospect theory is NOT correct?
o: Expected utility theory describes how a perfectly rational person should choose
Prospect theory evaluates outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point
Prospect theory describes how people ought to choose, so it is a normative model
Expected utility theory weighs the utility of each outcome by its probability
theme.spot: Normative = how we should choose; descriptive = how we do choose.
theme.why: Prospect theory is descriptive: it describes how people actually choose and why they break expected utility. Expected utility theory is the normative yardstick: utility times probability, for an ideal rational decision maker. The other three statements are correct.
theme.src: [LO D1, D3][IDQ DE2] Robinson-Riegler pp. 481-483

theme.q: Scenario 1: you lose your €25 museum ticket at the entrance. Scenario 2: you lose a €25 note on your way to buy the ticket. People are much less willing to pay €25 again in scenario 1. According to Matlin, what produces this difference?
o: The wording of the question, which presents one scenario as a gain and the other as a loss
The background context of the choice, which puts the lost money in a different mental account
The certainty effect, because the ticket was certain while the note was only probable
Anchoring, because the price of the first ticket serves as a starting point for the second
theme.spot: The money lost is identical; what differs is where it is booked.
theme.why: Matlin separates two framing factors: the background context and the wording. Here the wording is not about gains versus losses; the situation differs. A lost ticket is booked in the “museum account”, so a new ticket feels like paying €50 (psychological accounting). In the classic concert version 46% would buy again after losing the ticket and 88% after losing the cash.
theme.src: [LO D4][IDQ DE5] Matlin pp. 437-439 (Demonstration 12.7); Robinson-Riegler p. 486

theme.q: Judgement I: after seven reds in a row at roulette, a player bets on black because black is “due”. Judgement II: people estimate that murder causes more deaths than suicide, although the opposite is true. These judgements are
o: both due to the availability heuristic
both due to the representativeness heuristic
due to the availability and the representativeness heuristic, respectively
due to the representativeness and the availability heuristic, respectively
theme.spot: First: what should a random sequence look like? Second: what comes to mind easily?
theme.why: I is the gambler's fallacy: a short run is expected to look like a random process, so black seems due. That is representativeness. II: murders get much publicity, so examples come to mind easily and seem frequent (Lichtenstein et al., 1978). That is availability.
theme.src: [PAST-1] set1 'respectively' shape; Eysenck & Keane p. 626; Matlin & Farmer

theme.q: Tom is quiet, loves science fiction and spends his evenings building computers. Many people rate “Tom is an accountant who plays online games” as more likely than “Tom is an accountant”. What is this error, and where does it come from?
o: The conjunction fallacy, caused by the representativeness heuristic
The conjunction fallacy, caused by the anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic
Base-rate neglect, caused by the availability heuristic
The gambler's fallacy, caused by the representativeness heuristic
theme.spot: A combination (A and B) judged likelier than one of its parts (A).
theme.why: Every accountant who plays online games is also an accountant, so the combination can never be more likely: the conjunction fallacy. The added detail fits the description, so the combination looks more typical: representativeness, as in the Linda problem. The gambler's fallacy is about random sequences.
theme.src: [PAST-1][LO J5][IDQ ABC6] Matlin & Farmer; Eysenck & Keane

theme.q: What is the difference between the conjunction fallacy and the double conjunction fallacy?
o: In the double version the combination is judged likelier than each of its two parts
In the double version two people commit the fallacy about the same description
In the double version the fallacy is made twice in a row, before and after feedback
In the double version base rates are ignored as well as the conjunction rule
theme.spot: Count how many of the parts the combination is said to beat.
theme.why: In the conjunction fallacy “A and B” is judged likelier than one part. In the double conjunction fallacy it is judged likelier than both A and B separately. Crupi et al. (2018): 49% of medical experts judged “alcoholism and thalassemia” more probable than either alone.
theme.src: [IDQ ABC6] Eysenck & Keane (Crupi et al., 2018)

theme.q: Participants estimated how many seven-letter words in a 2,000-word passage end in -ing, or have n as the second-to-last letter. Estimates for -ing words were more than twice as high. What does this show?
o: Ease of generating examples drove the estimates, since -ing words are a subset of the other
Estimates followed resemblance to a typical English word, since -ing words look more like real words
Estimates were anchored on the first word that came to mind and were then adjusted too little
Estimates were correct, since -ing is the most frequent ending of seven-letter English words
theme.spot: Can the subset be bigger than the set? Then why was it judged bigger?
theme.why: Every -ing word has n as its second-to-last letter, so it is a subset and cannot be more frequent. Yet -ing words are much easier to generate, so they feel more frequent: the availability heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). Sternberg notes it also produces a conjunction-type error.
theme.src: [CORE] Sternberg et al. pp. 493, 497

theme.q:
Judge these statements about the hindsight bias.
I. Matlin explains it with anchoring and adjustment: the known outcome serves as a 100% anchor and people adjust too little.
II. In Carli's (1999) study, readers recalled story details that fitted the ending they had read, although those details were not in the story.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Two claims from the hindsight section: one explanation, one finding.
theme.why: Both are true. Knowing the outcome happened (100% certain) acts as an anchor, and people do not adjust their “I would have predicted it” downward enough. Carli showed the memory side: each group falsely “remembered” details that fitted the ending (rape or proposal), so the past is reconstructed to match what we know now.
theme.src: [PAST-1][LO J5][IDQ ABC10] Matlin pp. 444-446

theme.q:
Of 1,000 athletes, 20 used a banned drug. A test is positive for 18 of these 20 athletes, and also for 49 of the 980 clean athletes.
Test positiveTest negative
Used drug (20)182
Clean (980)49931
An athlete tests positive. What is the probability that this athlete used the drug (rounded to a whole percentage)?
theme.spot: Only the positive column matters: true positives divided by all positives.
theme.why: There are 18 + 49 = 67 positive tests, of which 18 are true: 18 / 67 = 27%. The tempting 90% is the test's hit rate (18 of 20), which ignores the base rate: clean athletes are so many that their false positives outnumber the true ones. Counting in natural frequencies like this makes the Bayesian answer easy (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).
theme.src: [LO J2][IDQ ABC9] Eysenck & Keane pp. 623-624, 629

theme.q: In the taxicab problem, 85% of the city's cabs are Green and 15% Blue. A witness who is correct 80% of the time says the cab in an accident was Blue. Most people say the chance it was Blue is 80%, while Bayes' theorem gives about 41%. What does this finding show?
o: People rely on the witness and neglect how rare Blue cabs are
People combine the base rate and the witness accuracy correctly
People distrust the witness and rely only on the base rate
People judge the cab Blue because Blue cabs are more available
theme.spot: The intuitive answer equals the witness accuracy.
theme.why: The answer of 80% uses only the witness and ignores the base rate (only 15% Blue). Because Green cabs are so common, a Green cab wrongly called Blue is likely, which brings the correct answer down to 41%. This is base-rate neglect (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972).
theme.src: [LO J2][IDQ ABC9] Eysenck & Keane pp. 623-624

theme.q: Which statement about overconfidence is NOT correct, according to the readings?
o: People who were 100% sure of their answers were right only about 80% of the time
In a large study, 77% of students were overconfident about general-knowledge answers
Experts such as physicists and political leaders are well calibrated about their own judgements
The planning fallacy is overconfidence about how quickly a project will be finished
theme.spot: Look for the claim that someone is protected from the bias.
theme.why: Overconfidence is widespread: political leaders overestimate their chances of success, and physicists and economists are overconfident about their theories (Matlin). The other statements are from the readings: Fischhoff et al. (1977) found 80% accuracy at 100% certainty, Stanovich (1999) 77% overconfident students, and the planning fallacy is overconfidence about time.
theme.src: [PAST-2][IDQ ABC4] Matlin pp. 440-443; Sternberg et al.

theme.q: A slot machine has paid out nothing in its last 40 rounds. A player keeps feeding it coins because “a win must be coming soon”. Each round is independent. Which error is this?
o: The hot hand belief
The gambler's fallacy
The sunk-cost effect
Anchoring and adjustment
theme.spot: A streak is expected to end, as if the machine remembers.
theme.why: The gambler's fallacy: after a run of one outcome, the opposite seems “due”, because a short sequence is expected to look random (representativeness). The machine has no memory. The hot hand belief is the reverse: a streak is expected to continue. Sunk cost would be “I have put in so much, I can't stop now”, which is not the reason given.
theme.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2] set1/set2 representativeness items; Eysenck & Keane; Sternberg et al.

theme.q: In expected utility theory, the principle of invariance states that
o: a choice should not depend on the way the same options are presented
a choice should not depend on outcomes that both options have in common
a choice should follow a consistent order, so A over B and B over C means A over C
a choice should favour an option that is at least as good in every outcome
theme.spot: Invariance: the preference stays the same across descriptions.
theme.why: Invariance: if you prefer A to B in one presentation, you should prefer A to B in any other presentation of the same options (Robinson-Riegler). The second option is cancellation, the third transitivity, the fourth dominance.
theme.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2][LO D1][IDQ DE6] Robinson-Riegler p. 482

theme.q: Lichtenstein and Slovic (1971, 1973) had people choose which of two gambles to play and set a selling price for each. People often chose one gamble but put a higher price on the other. What does this show?
o: Choice followed the chance of winning and price followed the amount, a violation of invariance
Choice and price both followed the amount to be won, which supports expected utility theory
Only students reversed their preferences; casino card dealers chose and priced consistently
People priced the gambles higher when they were described as gains rather than as losses
theme.spot: Preferring one gamble but valuing the other higher.
theme.why: A rational person should price highest the gamble they prefer. Instead choice tracked the probability of winning and price tracked the amount: a preference reversal, which Robinson-Riegler presents as a violation of invariance. The same result appeared in a Las Vegas casino with card dealers among the players.
theme.src: [LO D1][CORE] Robinson-Riegler pp. 482-483

m1.q:
Judge these statements.
I. If patients choose an operation more often when it is described as “90% survive” than as “10% die”, invariance is violated.
II. Expected utility theory predicts this difference, because losses weigh more than gains.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
m1.spot: Which theory predicts framing effects, and which forbids them?
m1.why: I is true: “90% survive” and “10% die” describe the same operation, so a different choice breaks invariance. II is false: expected utility theory forbids such a difference. The idea that losses weigh more is loss aversion from prospect theory, which is the theory that explains the effect.
m1.src: [PAST-1][PAST-2][LO D1, D4] Robinson-Riegler pp. 482-484 (framing in medical decisions)

m1.q: People judge it more likely that next year a river will flood a town in Limburg after heavy rain than that a river will flood a town somewhere in the Netherlands. Which error is this?
o: Hindsight bias
The conjunction fallacy
The gambler's fallacy
Anchoring and adjustment
m1.spot: A specific case (Limburg) judged more likely than the whole (the Netherlands).
m1.why: Limburg is part of the Netherlands, so a flood there can never be more likely than a flood anywhere in the country. Judging the vivid, specific case as more probable is the conjunction fallacy, like murders in Detroit versus Michigan. The specific story looks representative of floods, so it feels likelier.
m1.src: [PAST-1] set1 California item; Matlin & Farmer (Detroit vs Michigan)

m1.q: After weeks of seeing friends' holiday photos from Bali on social media, Mark estimates that Bali is the most popular holiday destination of Dutch people. In fact it is far from the top. Which heuristic best explains his estimate?
o: Representativeness
Availability
Anchoring and adjustment
Recognition
m1.spot: Frequency judged by how easily examples come to mind.
m1.why: Mark judges frequency by how easily examples come to mind: recent, repeated photos make Bali very available. Availability errs when recency and familiarity, rather than true frequency, drive retrieval. The recognition heuristic would apply if he knew only one of two destinations.

m1.q: Most people prefer €3,000 for sure over an 80% chance of €4,000. Yet most prefer a 20% chance of €4,000 over a 25% chance of €3,000. Which phenomenon explains this pattern?
o: Loss aversion
The certainty effect
Diminishing sensitivity
The reference point
m1.spot: Only the first pair contains a sure option, and only there do people play safe.
m1.why: Dividing both chances by four should not change the preference, yet it does. When one option is certain, it gets extra weight; once it is only probable (25%), the bigger prize wins. This is the certainty effect, the probability side of prospect theory. There are no losses here, so loss aversion does not apply.

m2.q: A recruiter compares candidates two at a time. She prefers Anna to Ben, and Ben to Chris. When Anna and Chris are compared, she prefers Chris. Which principle of expected utility theory is violated?
o: Invariance
Cancellation
Transitivity
Dominance
m2.spot: Follow the chain: does it close into a circle?
m2.why: Anna > Ben and Ben > Chris logically requires Anna > Chris. Preferring Chris makes the preferences circular, which violates transitivity. Invariance would need the same options described in two ways; cancellation concerns outcomes that two options share.

m2.q: Which feature of the prospect theory value function reflects loss aversion?
o: The curve is concave for gains and convex for losses
The curve is steeper on the loss side than on the gain side
The curve passes through a reference point instead of zero wealth
The curve flattens as gains and losses become larger
m2.why: Loss aversion is the steeper loss side: losing €50 drops value more than gaining €50 raises it. Concave for gains and convex for losses, and flattening further out, describe diminishing sensitivity. The reference point says gains and losses are judged from what you have now.

m2.q: Before an election, a commentator wrote that the challenger had little chance. After the challenger wins, he says he “saw it coming for months”, and in all honesty he believes this. Which bias is this?
o: Hindsight bias
Confirmation bias
The planning fallacy
Base-rate neglect
m2.spot: Outcome known, then the past “prediction” is rewritten.
m2.why: Hindsight bias: once the outcome is known, people believe they knew it all along. The known result serves as an anchor and memory is reconstructed to fit it (Carli, 1999). Confirmation bias is searching for evidence that supports a current belief; the planning fallacy is underestimating how long a project takes.

m2.q:
Judge these statements.
I. Expecting tails after five heads in a row with a fair coin is the gambler's fallacy.
II. After a statistical correction of the original analysis, several datasets show a modest real hot hand in basketball.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
m2.spot: Two streak beliefs: one always wrong, one not so clearly wrong.
m2.why: I is true: a fair coin has no memory, so “tails is due” is the gambler's fallacy. II is also true: Gilovich et al. (1985) found no hot hand, but Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) corrected a selection bias in that analysis and found a real but modest hot hand. So the gambler's fallacy stays a fallacy, the hot hand is less clearly one.
m2.src: [PAST-2] hot hand item; Eysenck & Keane (Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018)

m3.q: Most people prefer €500 for sure over a 50% chance of €1,000, although both have the same expected value. How does expected utility theory explain this?
o: Losing the gamble would feel much worse than winning it would feel good to them
The second €500 adds less utility than the first, so the gamble is worth less
The way the two options are worded makes the sure option look like a gain
People overestimate the chance of winning nothing because losses are vivid
m3.spot: Expected value is equal, so the answer must lie in how utility grows with money.
m3.why: With diminishing marginal utility the utility curve is concave: €1,000 is worth less than twice the utility of €500. The gamble's expected utility is therefore lower than that of the sure €500, so a rational chooser is risk averse. The first option is loss aversion, but nothing can be lost here; the third is framing, which expected utility theory does not allow to matter.
m3.src: [PAST-2][IDQ DE4] set2 diminishing marginal utility item

m3.q:
Judge these statements.
I. The cancellation principle says that an outcome which is the same in both options should not influence the choice.
II. The Allais paradox shows that people follow cancellation as soon as one of the options is certain.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
m3.spot: What does the certainty of one option do to cancellation?
m3.why: I is the correct definition of cancellation (independence). II is false: in the Allais paradox people break cancellation exactly when a certain option is available. Removing a shared chance from both options flips their choice, because the sure thing gets extra weight (the certainty effect).

m3.q: In a village there are 95 farmers for every 5 librarians. Sanne is described as shy, tidy and fond of books. Most people say she is probably a librarian. What do they neglect, and why?
o: The sample size, because the description is based on only one person
The base rate, because they judge by how much Sanne resembles a librarian
The base rate, because examples of shy farmers do not come to mind easily
The sample size, because the first description they read anchors the estimate
m3.spot: Numbers in the stem that nobody uses: how common each job is.
m3.why: With 19 farmers for every librarian, Sanne is most likely a farmer even if the description fits librarians better. People judge by resemblance to the stereotype (representativeness) and neglect the base rate, as in the lawyer-engineer problem (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973). The third option names the right error but the wrong heuristic.

m3.q: According to prospect theory, people tend to be
o: risk averse when options are framed as gains and risk seeking when framed as losses
risk seeking when options are framed as gains and risk averse when framed as losses
risk averse in both frames, but more strongly when options are framed as losses
risk seeking in both frames, but more strongly when options are framed as gains
m3.spot: Sure gain: keep it. Sure loss: gamble to avoid it.
m3.why: With a gain frame people take the sure thing (risk averse); with a loss frame they gamble to avoid a sure loss (risk seeking). The value curve explains this: concave for gains, convex for losses. In the Asian disease problem 72% chose the sure option for lives saved and 78% the risky one for deaths.
m3.src: [LO D4][IDQ DE4] Matlin p. 440; Robinson-Riegler p. 483
